input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-142: Computer Science II. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course delves further into problem solving by continuing the discussion of data structure use and design, but now from an object- oriented perspective. Key topics include more information on tree and graph structures, nested data structures, objects, classes, inheritance, interfaces, object-oriented collection class libraries for abstract data types (e.g. stacks, queues, maps, and trees), and static vs. dynamic data types. Concepts of object-oriented design are a large part of the course. Software qualities related to object orientation, namely cohesion, minimal coupling, modifiability, and extensibility, are all introduced in this course, as well as a few elementary object-oriented design patterns. Input and output streams, graphical user interfaces, and exception handling are covered. Students will also be introduced to a modern integrated software development environment (IDE). Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-141 with a grade of C- or better or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture/Lab 6 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: GE: Elective, GE: Mathematical Perspective, NTID Math Processes, SMTL: Science/Math Literacy Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer Every beat must be directly relevant to that catalog description. Prefer the RIT catalog source for scope claims. Use a supplemental source only when its cited claim teaches a named course topic; never use an unrelated source merely to fill a claim slot. Keep production directions exclusively in visualDirection and never say phrases such as 'on screen', 'show on screen', 'cut to', or 'camera' in narration. Regeneration revision 4: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[opendsa-programming-foundations]
Programming begins with precise problem statements, input and output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax. Variables represent values and state, expressions compute values, and control structures select or repeat operations. Functions decompose a solution into named operations with parameters and results. Recursion solves a problem through smaller instances and requires a base case. Lists represent ordered sequences, stacks use last-in first-out access, queues use first-in first-out access, trees represent hierarchy, and graphs represent connected entities. Searching and sorting algorithms depend on representation and invariants. Correctness arguments, tests, tracing, and debugging compare intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases.

[python-language-reference]
The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics. Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace. Programs should be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, contracts, tests, and observable behavior. Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns.

[rit-csci-142]
This course delves further into problem solving by continuing the discussion of data structure use and design, but now from an object- oriented perspective. Key topics include more information on tree and graph structures, nested data structures, objects, classes, inheritance, interfaces, object-oriented collection class libraries for abstract data types (e.g. stacks, queues, maps, and trees), and static vs. dynamic data types. Concepts of object-oriented design are a large part of the course. Software qualities related to object orientation, namely cohesion, minimal coupling, modifiability, and extensibility, are all introduced in this course, as well as a few elementary object-oriented design patterns. Input and output streams, graphical user interfaces, and exception handling are covered. Students will also be introduced to a modern integrated software development environment (IDE). Programming projects will be required. Prerequisites: CSCI-141 with a grade of C- or better or equivalent course. Contact Hours: Lecture/Lab 6 It may be used to fulfill one of the following: GE: Elective, GE: Mathematical Perspective, NTID Math Processes, SMTL: Science/Math Literacy Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: Programming begins with precise problem statements, input and output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax, where functions decompose solutions into named, self-
beats.example: To sort a list of student grades, first define the input (unsorted list) and output (sorted list), then design a recursive merge algorithm before writing any Python code.
beats.title: 1. Problem Decomposition and Algorithmic Foundations
beats.visualDirection: Display a flowchart showing the decomposition of a complex problem into smaller sub-problems, with arrows pointing from the main problem to three distinct function blocks labeled 'Input Validation', 'Core Algorithm', and 'Output Formatting'

beats.claim: Trees represent hierarchy and graphs represent connected entities; both are fundamental structures for organizing data in object-oriented systems, supporting nested data structures
beats.example: A family tree is modeled as a tree where each node is a Person object, while a social network is modeled as a graph where nodes are User objects and edges represent friendships.
beats.title: 2. Data Structures: Trees and Graphs
beats.visualDirection: Render a side-by-side comparison: left side shows a binary tree diagram with labeled nodes, right side shows a directed graph with nodes and weighted edges

beats.claim: Python objects have identity, a type, and a value; classes define these attributes and behaviors, and inheritance allows subclasses to reuse and extend parent functionality
beats.example: Define a base class 'Vehicle' with attributes 'speed' and 'color'; create a subclass 'ElectricCar' that inherits these and adds a 'battery_level' attribute.
beats.title: 3. Objects, Classes, and Inheritance
beats.visualDirection: Show a UML class diagram with a 'Vehicle' class containing attributes and methods, and an arrow pointing from 'ElectricCar' to 'Vehicle' labeled 'extends'

beats.claim: Interfaces define contracts for behavior without implementation details, enabling polymorphism; object-oriented collection libraries provide ready-made implementations for stacks,
beats.example: Define an interface 'QueueInterface' with methods 'enqueue' and 'dequeue'; use the built-in collections.deque as the concrete implementation for a queue in a banking system.
beats.title: 4. Interfaces and Abstract Data Types
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a contract diagram where multiple classes (e.g., 'BankAccount', 'Transaction') implement the 'QueueInterface' box, with dotted lines indicating the interface relationship

beats.claim: Static types are determined at compile time and enforce strict structure, while dynamic types (like Python) are resolved at runtime, allowing flexible object manipulation
beats.example: In a statically typed language, a variable declared as 'int' cannot hold a string; in Python, the same variable can be reassigned to any object type without recompilation.
beats.title: 5. Static vs. Dynamic Data Types
beats.visualDirection: Split screen: left side shows a compiler error message for a type mismatch, right side shows a Python REPL where a variable changes type seamlessly

beats.claim: High cohesion means a class has a single, well-defined responsibility; low coupling means classes depend minimally on each other, both critical for modifiability
beats.example: A 'PaymentProcessor' class should only handle payment logic (high cohesion) and should not directly instantiate 'EmailSender' (low coupling); instead, it receives an interface for sending notifications.
beats.title: 6. Software Qualities: Cohesion and Coupling
beats.visualDirection: Draw two boxes: one labeled 'High Cohesion' with tightly related methods inside, another labeled 'Low Coupling' with loose connections to external modules

beats.claim: Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate, allowing robust error management in object-oriented programs
beats.example: When dividing by zero in a financial calculation, raise a ZeroDivisionError; catch it in a try-except block to log the error and return a default value.
beats.title: 7. Exception Handling and Control Flow
beats.visualDirection: Show a code snippet with a try-except block, highlighting the exception being raised and the handler executing, with a visual indicator of flow diversion

beats.claim: Input and output streams provide a unified interface for reading from and writing to various sources, while graphical user interfaces enable interactive program interaction
beats.example: Read user input via sys.stdin stream, process it, and display results using a simple Tkinter window with a label and button.
beats.title: 8. Input/Output Streams and GUI Basics
beats.visualDirection: Display a mock IDE window with a console pane showing input/output streams and a separate GUI pane with a button and text field

beats.claim: A modern integrated software development environment (IDE) combines code editing, debugging, and project management, essential for efficient object-oriented development
beats.example: Using PyCharm, a student can set breakpoints, inspect object attributes in the debugger, and refactor code with a single click.
beats.title: 9. Modern IDE Integration
beats.visualDirection: Screenshot-style graphic of an IDE interface showing the editor, debugger panel, and project explorer, with annotations pointing to key features

beats.claim: Correctness arguments, tests, tracing, and debugging compare intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases, ensuring reliable software
beats.example: Before submitting a project, run unit tests for edge cases (e.g., empty lists, null objects) and trace execution to verify exception handling paths.
beats.title: 10. Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Present a checklist graphic with items: 'Define Pre/Post Conditions', 'Write Unit Tests', 'Trace Execution', 'Review Boundary Cases', each with a checkbox

learningObjectives: Identify and apply core object-oriented design principles (cohesion, coupling, inheritance) to structure code for modifiability and extensibility.
Select appropriate abstract data types (stacks, queues, trees, graphs) and implement them using object-oriented collection libraries.
Design and implement exception handling and input/output streams within a modern IDE to manage runtime errors and user interaction.
